s50m:S1Q04F.q: How would you reduce the sorting cost for millions of customers while preserving the tie rule?
s50m:S1Q04F.label: gemini-3.5-flash-lite_fturn-s50m-A
s50m:S1Q04F.spoken: To avoid a full sort on millions of records, I use linear-time partial selection like argpartition to isolate just the top candidates. I attach the original index as a secondary key for deterministic tie-breaking. Then, we only run a full sort on that small subset, cutting our compute cost while preserving the exact tie rules.

s50m:S1Q06F.q: How would you index those tables, and what changes if historical records can be corrected after ingestion?
s50m:S1Q06F.label: gemini-3.5-flash-lite_fturn-s50m-A
s50m:S1Q06F.spoken: I'd place a composite B-tree index on customer ID and timestamp in the events table for fast filtered joins, and a primary index on customer ID for snapshots. s50m:S2Q05F.q: Construct an example where that greedy policy gives poor coverage, and tell me how you would incorporate redundancy or multi hop dependence
s50m:S2Q05F.label: gemini-3.5-flash-lite_fturn-s50m-A
s50m:S2Q05F.spoken: Imagine a financial compliance audit where three different sections of a lengthy contract discuss liability limits using completely different legal phrasing; a greedy relevance-first sort might pull the top three scoring chunks from the exact same paragraph because they share the highest semantic overlap with the query, leaving the other two critical clauses out. To fix that, I modify the selection loop to score candidates using Maximal Marginal Relevance, penalizing chunks that are too textually or semantically similar to ones already picked so every added piece introduces fresh coverage. The key dependencies driving this are your embedding model's distance threshold for novelty and the inference latency overhead of running pairwise similarity checks across the candidate pool on the fly.

s50m:S2Q08F.q: How do you prove the replacement index is sufficiently complete and current before you send production traffic to it?
s50m:S2Q08F.label: gemini-3.5-flash-lite_fturn-s50m-A
s50m:S2Q08F.spoken: I run shadow validation by re-running our golden evaluation set against both indexes in parallel to verify parity on retrieval hit rates and precision. I also check metadata counts and ingestion logs to guarantee that every document from the source partition is indexed before we route traffic.

s50m:D1.q: How would you index those tables, and what changes if historical records can be corrected after ingestion?
s50m:D1.label: gemini-3.5-flash-lite_fturn-s50m-A
s50m:D1.spoken: I'd start with standard B-tree indexes on primary keys, foreign keys, and high-cardinality filter columns, plus GIN indexes for any JSON metadata payloads. If historical records can be corrected, I'd switch from destructive in-place updates to an append-only temporal table design using valid-from and valid-to timestamps. That ensures corrections are safely recorded as new versions while preserving audit trails, and lets us easily invalidate downstream cache layers or recompute aggregates from the exact mutation timestamp.

s50m:D2.q: Construct an example where that greedy policy gives poor coverage, and tell me how you would incorporate redundancy or multi hop dependence
s50m:D2.label: gemini-3.5-flash-lite_fturn-s50m-A
s50m:D2.spoken:
Imagine a financial audit where a greedy retrieval policy grabs the three most textually similar sections from an executive summary; it achieves high local similarity but completely misses the tax table appendix required for the final calculation. 

To incorporate redundancy and multi-hop dependence, I use agentic query decomposition in LangGraph alongside Maximal Marginal Relevance, ensuring each retrieval step fetches novel evidence conditioned on prior findings rather than duplicating top results. 

The key dependencies driving this are the shared state graph memory and deterministic tool checks that verify whether a fetched chunk actually resolves the missing entity before the agent moves to synthesis.

s50m:D3.q: How do you prove the replacement index is sufficiently complete and current before you send production traffic to it?
s50m:D3.label: gemini-3.5-flash-lite_fturn-s50m-A
s50m:D3.spoken: I validate a replacement index through count parity, evaluation regressions, and canary routing. First, I verify document and vector counts match the source store. Second, I run a golden test set to ensure retrieval metrics like Hit Rate don't regress. Finally, I canary a fraction of live traffic to monitor real-world performance before full cutover.
